content.thinking:
I need to write this file carefully in one pass without testing, using robust part geometries like lathe, extrude, and sweep. Since parts without bones need to attach to a root, I'll create a base joint at the origin to serve as that required root attachment point.

For the design, I'm going League-style: saturated, glowing treasure using toon-style cel paints for large flat surfaces to keep colors manageable. The scene layout has a coin mound at the center, a chest with an open hinged lid at the back, and a scattered arrangement of crowns, goblets, gems, and coin stacks around it. I'm building the mound as a lathe shape from a rounded profile curve, painted with layered gold scale textures to mimic coin piles.

For the scattered coins, I'm scattering small cylinder discs across the mound surface using surface sampling, computing orientation for each hit by aiming along the surface normal, then merging all coin instances by color group into a few combined geometry parts to stay within part limits.

For a few hero coins, I'm thinking about adding visible face detail — considering texture-mapped cylinders versus layering a separate circular decal plane in front of a tilted cylinder so the face art doesn't bleed onto the coin's edge, then defining a helper to build these standing, textured coins.

Now I'm positioning the treasure chest relative to the coin mound, setting its box dimensions and placement so it sits partly sunk into the pile near the floor without clipping, and sketching out a wood-plank paint pattern for its body using vertical grain stripes.

Adding iron bands and lid hinge geometry...

Working through the rotation math confirms -110° about the X axis swings the lid upward and slightly back, which is the direction I want. I'll build all lid parts in closed position first, then apply that pose to the lidHinge bone, defining the hinge joint at the appropriate position relative to the base.

Now I'm figuring out the lid's half-cylinder geometry: using a cylinder shape with partial theta sweep, then rotating it 90° about Z so the curved face opens upward rather than sideways. Tracking how the local axes transform under that rotation to make sure the arc faces the correct direction...

Since the partial cylinder leaves the inner side open, I'm adding a thin flat box as the lid's underside panel to cover the gap, positioning it relative to the hinge point and chest depth so it sits flush against the curved shell.

Now I'm working out the chest body dimensions and positioning the lid cylinder's center accordingly, then adding a rounded gold mound for coins piled inside the open chest.

For the decorative hardware, I'm trying to figure out how to sweep thin strap shapes along an arc over the lid's curved surface, defining start and end points in local model space before the whole chest gets posed.

Still working out the lock plate and front straps...

Now I'm adding corner brackets and merged rivet spheres by color, then figuring out how to paint the body like wooden planks with darker seam lines at regular intervals and grain-based shading between them.

For the crown, I'm placing it on top of the coin pile mound, sizing it at roughly radius 0.13 with a slight exaggeration for the LoL style, and planning the lathe base band, five extruded points, gems, and inner velvet lining, tilted slightly for a natural resting look.

Writing crown geometry...

Adding rim torus sweeps at top and bottom of the crown band, then shaping a velvet dome cap that sits inside the band below the spike tips using a cel-shaded red-purple lathe profile, and starting on the goblet geometry with a foot disc and stem.

Checking the inner and outer profile points near the knob don't cross by comparing their x-values at matching heights—confirming the inner curve stays safely inside the outer at each y-level along the stem.

Now I'm adding a ring of small gem spheres around the goblet's bowl, placing them evenly spaced using a ring helper and attaching each one to its corresponding point.

For positioning the goblets on the mound, I'm raycasting downward from above to find the terrain height at each location, falling back to a default if the ray misses. I'm setting up one upright gold goblet and one tipped-over silver goblet lying on its side with a slight rotation, approximating where spilled coins would land near it.

For the gem clusters, I'm using octahedron geometry scaled along the y-axis to create faceted crystal shapes, assigning each a gem color (ruby, sapphire, emerald, amethyst, topaz) with a glow effect, then scattering them across the mound surface oriented along the surface normal with randomized rotation and scale.

Now I'm planning a background crystal cluster using hex-prism spikes with pointed tips, positioning five amethyst/cyan crystals of varying heights behind-left for a glowing, LoL-style aesthetic, and considering color banding to give each spike a lighter glowing tip.

I'm also figuring out coin stacks—clusters of jittered cylinders merged per stack to simulate loose coin piles, placing them on the mound's sloped ground using the groundY function so they sit naturally on the terrain rather than floating.

Now I'm designing a money sack as a lathe shape with a tied neck and rounded body, carefully plotting the outline points to form a closed bag silhouette without any self-intersecting edges.

Writing circle helper for the tie rope, then adding a gold gem decal plane positioned on the sack's front bulge.

I'm skipping a sword or map since the theme is coins and jewels. I'm sketching out a draping necklace and pearl strand hanging over the chest's front edge, building the chain path and pendant placement using swept points.

Still writing jewelry geometry...

Finishing the coin emblem SVG...

I also want some loose coins scattered, plus a stack of gold ingots made from extruded trapezoid shapes, layered pyramid-style near the goblets, and I'm now working out their positions in the layout.

I'm now placing each prop: the chest centered behind, the crown resting tilted on the mound, a gold goblet upright, a silver one nearby, and a third tipped goblet further along, then checking the ingot stack and coin sack positions against the mound's slope so everything sits naturally without clipping.

Now I'm scattering crystals, several small coin stacks with mixed gold and silver colors and varying coin counts, plus a scattered layer of gems across the mound filtered to stay above a certain height. I'm also adding a tiny gem ring prop lying flat near the front, and considering a cascade of coins spilling out from the chest's open lid for extra detail.

For the mound surface itself, I'm building it as a lathe shape and wrapping a skin surface over it so I can scatter props onto it using raycasts. I'm writing a helper function that takes each scatter hit's position and normal, orients a coin to align with the surface normal while adding slight random tilt and spin, then groups the coin geometries by color so they can be merged efficiently later.

Now I'm thinking through the merge step — combining all same-color coin geometries into single meshes using mergeGeometries, then adding them as parts with flat gold and silver tones. I'm sizing the scatter density at 260 coins across the mound with a minimum distance filter restricted to upward-facing normals, accepting some coins will end up hidden inside the chest geometry since that's a minor visual overlap I can live with.

Then I refine the filter to explicitly exclude the chest's footprint so coins don't scatter underneath it, while leaving room for the crown and goblet to rest naturally on the coin pile. For gems, I'm scattering around 22 pieces using octahedron geometry stretched vertically, colored from a five-gem palette, with randomized sizes between 0.7x and 1.4x scale, plus three larger hero gems placed deliberately at prominent positions on the mound front for visual focal points.

Now I'm checking my imports carefully to avoid unused-import errors—keeping only what's needed like glow, cel, paint utilities, arc, catmull, svg, and frame—while deciding on paint treatments like a mottled stone disc and a steel-toned iron chest. Then I start writing the build export with metadata including a name, description, and style tag.

Defining gold and silver color palette and plank seam patterns...

Now setting up the treasure chest skeleton with base and hinge joints for the lid.

Still building geometry...

I'm setting up a ground-height function that raycasts downward onto the mound, and starting on the chest body as a painted box geometry positioned above it.

Now I'm adding a heap of coins on top of the chest using a hemisphere-shaped sphere scaled flat, positioned to sit just above the box top, with gems and pearls scattered across it. Next I'm building wood trim corner posts as thin boxes...

Still placing trim pieces...

I'm placing the keyhole detail with a dark box and sphere on the lock, plus a glowing octahedron gem above it. For the lid, I'm considering a hasp tongue plate but deciding to skip it since it would overlap the lock and conflict with the lid's hinge rotation, so the lock plate alone will serve that role.

Now I'm positioning the lid as a half-cylinder attached to a hinge bone, working out the rotation math so the cylinder's axis aligns correctly along the chest's width with its open side facing down, using a semicircular cross-section for the curved lid shape.

Next I'm adding steel straps as arc sweeps across the lid at a few x positions, computing their path geometry and rectangular cross-section, then attaching gold rivets along those straps using a helper that walks points along the arc path and places sphere parts at each frame.

I'm sizing the rivet spheres so they sit just slightly protruding from the strap surface, adding an inner velvet board under the lid to cover the underside when open, and considering whether to add a gold crest gem on the lid front before deciding to skip it.

Now I'm working out the hinge rotation for the lid, applying a -105° pose so it swings open and sits behind the chest, then checking the resulting height and depth extents of the open lid to make sure it clears the body properly.

Checking the overall silhouette: crystals reach up to about .7 and the open lid tops out near .85, so I'm sketching out the crystal base positions and their directional offsets around the chest's back corner next.

Writing crystal spike code...

Now I'm setting up a goblet function that takes position, body color, gem color, and a tipped flag.

I'll scatter a few spilled gold coins near the goblet's rim, placing them on the ground with upward-facing normals, then add a ring of gems around the upright goblets' bands using rotated loop positions.

Adding gem spheres and rim band...

For colors I'll use the cel-shading helper consistently across the goblet materials, like gold, for a flat toon look, then move on to building the crown helper as planned.

Positioning the crown with a tilted transform on top of the coins, then laying out its lathe profile points...

Still writing crown geometry...

Positioning the four band gems around the ring, orienting each octahedron outward with a flattened scale so they sit like embedded jewels along the circumference.

I'm then adding a closed gold rim ring using circle points swept with a tube, followed by a lathe-generated velvet dome sitting at the crown's base, sized so it stays inside the band and keeps the spikes as the tallest feature.

Now I'm oversizing the crown radius deliberately for a stylized look, writing a circle-points helper for generating ring/crown vertex arrays, and extruding gold ingot bars from flat outlines stacked in a small pyramid formation, working out the rotation and extrusion directions for each bar.

I'm placing the gold bars (plus one silver variant on top) at a position near the mound edge, then planning a lathed sack shape nearby that overlaps the mound.

For the sack I'm positioning it to sit above the chest without colliding, adding a tie-ring sweep near the neck with small spike tassels, and placing a gem emblem decal on the front face of the bulge.

For the top of the sack I'm adding a small heap of spilled coins using a flattened gold hemisphere plus a coin pair glimpse at the opening.

Then I'm planning a ring with a tiny torus band and a glowing octahedral gem on top, plus a necklace built from a catmull-rom path with gold chain segments and pearl spheres distributed along it, ending in a teardrop pendant gem.

I'm now computing the actual pearl heap geometry — figuring out where the mound of pearls intersects with the chest curve, since the mound bulges up near the center and partially buries the front of the chest shape, so I need coordinates that account for that overlap rather than floating pearls above the surface.

With the chest front at that recalculated position, height comes to roughly .12 — better. I'm working out the base disc's radius and center so it fully covers the mound's extent in z and x, then checking the chest's back edge sits flush with the floor, before placing crystal positions along the back.

I'm repositioning the sack so it sits outside the mound's radius and redefining the mound's center and height profile using a lathe outline, so the ground height follows the surface automatically. I also realize the mound footprint overlaps the chest's base, so I need to filter out any coins that would spawn inside the chest's z-range near the center.

Now I'm placing the chest components: the body box at a shifted z-center, a hinge joint at the back edge, a lid cylinder and arc positioned relative to the chest center, and a heap sphere for the coin pile sitting against the lid.

Working out exact lock, strap, rim, hinge, and post positions relative to the chest's new z-offset, then placing a pearl strand that dips down into the coin mound near the front rim.

Now I'm plotting a second gold chain path slightly offset from the pearls, ending in an emerald pendant positioned near the mound's surface so it appears partially buried in the coins.

I'm also checking placements for the crown and goblets against the mound's radial height profile, making sure each item sits correctly on the terrain at its given coordinates.

Checking placement distances for the sack and crystal clusters relative to the disc center to make sure everything stays within the platform radius.

Repositioning the emerald near the goblet cluster and finalizing the gem placements, then moving on to writing the full typed code for the coin and glow functions, hit scattering logic, and a simple SVG gem emblem for the sack.

Now I'm adding flat gold coin decals scattered across the mound, using cylinders with small circular face decals offset slightly along the surface normal to sit flush on top.

I'm building a stacking function that generates coin piles by jittering positions and heights, grouping the cylinder geometries by color (gold, silver, darker/lighter gold variants) so they can be merged efficiently at the end.

Finishing the merge loop by combining geometries per color group and attaching them to the base part, then double-checking that all imports are actually used to avoid typecheck errors. I'm also setting up a paint function for the plank texture based on vertical position bands.

Now I'm defining a generic circle-point helper that generates points around a circle in local space with an optional matrix transform, useful for building the crown geometry.

I'm also planning a sweep helper for closed paths using Catmull-Rom curves through Vector3 points, plus a gem-sphere helper that creates glowing octahedron shapes positioned and scaled at given points, relying on the default flat-normal computation for low-detail octahedra.

I'm now sketching out part naming and coloring conventions -- wood cel colors for the chest, steel cylinders for hinge barrels, rivets placed along a path using a callback that samples frame points, and strap sweeps with varying cross-section widths along their length.

Working through arc orientation for the strap sweep to make sure the binormal and normal axes line up correctly with the path geometry, then planning the gold-colored heap of coins using scaled spheres and a shared color palette.
